pass_a_gloss: [Label 1 Cor 1:1-2.] He set this forth not simply, but in order to show that it is God's will that all be called after Christ and that there be apostles. At the same time he ranks with himself one known to the Corinthians, and he puts down the conceit of those who are lifted up over words (eloquence). He joins together the division that had badly come about, calling them one church, and of God; and he places first 'in Christ Jesus', not 'in so-and-so and so-and-so'. One must look at how in a few phrases he often mentions Christ Jesus, teaching from the very preface that it is fitting to be named from no one other than from our Lord Jesus Christ, and healing the wound from the splits of the different names by the continual remembrance of Jesus Christ. 'To those sanctified in Christ Jesus.' Not a man sanctified you, he says, but God in Christ. For if you call on a man, he says, be called from him; but if on Jesus Christ, be named from the one whom you call on (ὀνομάζον read as imperative ὀνομάζου). And well (is said) 'with all who call on': for not you alone, but all who believe everywhere call on Christ, and are named from him, not from men. So do not alone act strangely by bringing in an impious novelty. And he did not say 'with all who call the name' but 'who call on', showing the Son of God to be God; for one calls on God. 'In every place, theirs and ours.' If every place is calling on Jesus Christ, imitate the many, and do not alone do something strange beside the others. And 'theirs and ours' is fitted to 'the Lord', in place of: both we who write and you who enjoy the letters have one Christ Jesus. [Label 1 Cor 1:3-6.] From whom you have the grace and the peace, from him be named (ὀμομάζεσθε, read ὀνομάζεσθε). For the positings of these, taken up even before the proof and the exercise of the contests, [damaged verb: ἀπο...εισιν] to the thing being sought. And this is no less toward the correcting of the matters lying before (him): for if the grace is from our Lord Jesus Christ and not from men, from him, he says, it is fitting to be named. He remains on the same thing. For if wealth is from him, if knowledge from him, why do you put on yourselves the name of one as teacher, of another as having baptized, of another as presiding, of another as supplying? Therefore going forward he says: for what do you have that you did not receive, and if you also received, why do you boast as not having received? (1 Cor 4:7). 'In every word.' Since there is a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge (1 Cor 12:8) and many words of gifts, for this reason he says 'in every word and all knowledge'. Since also of knowledge the differences are many, (he adds) 'and all knowledge'. It was written to Greeks, who had not received together the Old and the New, and who were acquiring the knowledge from both sides: 'even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you.' [Label 1 Cor 1:8-9.] Those needing confirmation are already (thereby) incomplete. So he showed that they need correction, giving thanks for what they received, correcting for what they did not fulfil. 'God is faithful, through whom you were called.' Since he said 'God will confirm', he added 'God is faithful' - for God who is able to supply these things is true - 'through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son': not into a man's fellowship but into the fellowship of his Son. Why, having left being named from the Son into whose fellowship you were called, are you named from men? Again, 'through whom' is placed of the Father, not only of the Son. And it is no lowering for the Father, since through him we are called into the fellowship of his Son. For neither, (since) it is written in the (letter) to the Romans that through him and from him and into him are all things (Rom 11:36), is God then greater than himself because of 'from whom', and less than himself because of 'through whom'. So just as (these words) lying upon the same person do not make the same one less and greater than himself, so neither does 'through whom' said of him make the Son less. When he met the contest itself, so as to persuade (them) not from (men to be named ... continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: On 1 Corinthians 1:1–2: He did not put this at the head of the letter idly. He wanted to show that it is God's will for everyone to bear the name of Christ, and for there to be apostles. At once he sets beside himself a man the Corinthians knew, and he deflates the conceit of those who were proud of their eloquence. He binds up the division that had wrongly arisen by calling them one church, and God's church. And he puts "in Christ Jesus" first, not "in this man" or "in that one." Notice how often, in a few lines, he names Christ Jesus. From the very opening he teaches that we should take our name from no one but our Lord Jesus Christ, and by naming Jesus Christ again and again he heals the wound left by the split into rival names.

"To those sanctified in Christ Jesus." No man sanctified you, he says, but God in Christ. If you call on a man, he says, take your name from him; but if you call on Jesus Christ, take your name from the one you call on. "With all who call on" is well put. You are not the only ones; all believers everywhere call on Christ and are named after him, not after men. So do not be the only ones to stand out by bringing in an impious novelty. Notice too that he did not say "with all who call the name," but "who call on," and so shows that the Son of God is God, for it is God that one calls on. "In every place, theirs and ours": if every place calls on Jesus Christ, follow the many, and do not be the only ones to do something odd, apart from everyone else. "Theirs and ours" goes with "Lord." It means: we who write and you who enjoy the letter have one Christ Jesus.

On 1 Corinthians 1:3–6: Take your name from the one from whom you have grace and peace. Setting these words down even before the proof and the exercise of debate [bears] on the question at issue. And this does as much as anything to set the present faults right: if grace comes from our Lord Jesus Christ and not from men, he says, it is fitting to be named after him. He presses the same point. If wealth comes from him and knowledge comes from him, why do you give yourselves the name of one man as your teacher, of another as the one who baptized you, of another as your leader, and of yet another as your benefactor? That is why he says further on, "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?" (1 Corinthians 4:7).

"In every word." There is a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge (1 Corinthians 12:8), and there are many words of gifts, so he says, "in every word and all knowledge." And since knowledge also comes in many kinds, he adds "and all knowledge." The letter was written to Greeks, who had not received the Old and the New together, and who were gaining knowledge from both: "even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you."

On 1 Corinthians 1:8–9: Whoever needs to be confirmed is not yet complete. So he showed that they need correcting, giving thanks for what they had received and correcting them for what they had left undone. "God is faithful, through whom you were called." Having said that God will confirm them, he went on, "God is faithful" (for God, who can give these things, is true), "through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son": not into fellowship with a man, but into the fellowship of his Son. Why then do you give up being named after the Son, into whose fellowship you were called, and take your names from men? Notice again that "through whom" is said of the Father, not only of the Son. It does not lower the Father that we are called through him into the fellowship of his Son. Romans says, "through him and from him and to him are all things" (Romans 11:36), yet that does not make God greater than himself because of "from whom" and less than himself because of "through whom." Said of one and the same person, these words do not make him both less and greater than himself; in the same way "through whom," said of the Son, does not make the Son less.
When he came to the contest itself, to persuade them not to take their names from…

lemmas.gloss: be named after, take one's name from
act strangely, stand out as odd

choices.term: ὡς γνώριμον τοῖς Κορινθίοις ἑαυτῷ συντάττει
choices.english: sets beside himself a man the Corinthians knew
choices.why: The Greek does not name Sosthenes (1:1); the English does not add the name.
rejected: He arranges himself as being known (old reading; wrong subject)

choices.why: Both forms are misprints for ὀνομάζου / ὀνομάζεσθε; the parallel καλοῦ (imperative) and the argument call for a command.
The verb is damaged in the copy-text; the bracketed word is a guess at the sense and is noted.

choices.term: οὐδὲ γὰρ ... ἤδη ὁ θεὸς ... μείζων ἑαυτοῦ
choices.english: Romans says ... yet that does not make God greater than himself
choices.why: The negation governs the conclusion, not the quotation; the old English said Romans did not contain the verse.
rejected: it has not been written concerning the Romans

choices.why: Edition labels 1 Kor 1,1-2, 1,3-6, 1,8-9 match the lemmas; the closing note (on 1:10) has no label in the edition and none is invented.
